A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feature-learning study. The main text, equations, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original synthetic and Noisy-MNIST experiments, including learning trajectories, losses, classification accuracy, and denoising visualizations.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A retain these original experimental results, including the additional SNR settings, diffusion time, and ten-class MNIST experiments.

M1.justification: The quadratic two-layer networks, diffusion weight sharing, classification heads, DDPM and classification objectives, and gradient-descent procedures are retained. The revised weight decomposition changes the theoretical analysis, not the learning algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic two-patch data, binary Noisy-MNIST, and ten-class Noisy-MNIST. The additional SNR conditions and diffusion time t = 0.8 were already present in v1's Appendix A.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain the same diffusion-versus-classification comparisons, including the ten-class classifier adaptation. Newly cited research is not added as evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The reported data construction, sample counts, network configurations, noise schedules, and evaluation measures remain unchanged. The newly stated diffusion learning rate and training length document the existing experiment rather than establish a changed protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix A retains the same SNR sensitivity analysis, additional diffusion-time experiment, generalization comparisons, and input-gradient/denoising case studies. Their plots and substantive analyses are unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added probability statement in the diffusion theorem concerns theoretical guarantees, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The numerical plots and appendix findings are retained. Section 5.2 corrects v1's statement that high-SNR classification predominantly learns noise to say it predominantly learns signal, matching the existing Figure 8(c) and Appendix A.3. This is a corrected result description, not a performance improvement.

T1.justification: Conditions 3.1 and D.1 substantially revise dimension, initialization, noise, and width assumptions; the diffusion theorem now explicitly requires m = Theta(1). Appendix D introduces a varying initialization coefficient, a new Lemma D.6, and initialization-direction dynamics and stationarity equations. Lemma 4.2 and its appendix proof replace the previous second-stage time bound with one depending on initialization, dimension, and noise. These materially revise the central diffusion argument.

C1.justification: The central claim that diffusion learns more balanced features while classification preferentially learns dominant features remains. However, v2 removes the abstract's assertion that this comparison holds 'under identical settings,' qualifying the framing alongside the separately stated theoretical width requirements.

C2.justification: Appendix D replaces the statement that diffusion imposes no width restriction with an explicit constant-width limitation. Section 5.1 also removes the claim that the synthetic settings satisfy Condition 3.1. The conclusion adds prospective applications to conditional and latent diffusion, other objectives and optimizers, and flow matching; the principal feature-learning interpretation remains.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 newly states that synthetic diffusion training uses learning rate 0.5 and 40,000 iterations. The 3,000-sample classification test set is moved from the main text to Appendix A.1, so that disclosure is retained rather than newly added.

R1.justification: V2 adds six references, including work by Han et al. (2025), Okawa et al. (2024), and Yang et al. (2025), and connects the framework to feature composition and dependence. Chatterji and Long (2021) and Chen et al. (2022) are removed. The main positioning relative to diffusion theory, autoencoders, and representation learning remains.

P1.justification: V2 edits and condenses the main-text prose, adds Setup/Results labels in Section 5, recasts existing discussion as Remark 4.1, and adds acknowledgements. The overall section sequence and appendix organization remain substantially the same.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted into the ICLR 2025 template, changing typography, margins, title and affiliation placement, recurring headers, and citation styling. Figures are resized and repacked across the main text and Appendix A. Figures 1–15 remain, and all 37 embedded image assets are unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 improves the precision and auditability of the theoretical argument by explicitly tracking initialization-direction dynamics and revising the associated bounds and assumptions. It also supplies missing diffusion training settings and corrects the high-SNR result description. These gains come with narrower theoretical applicability, particularly constant diffusion width; the conflicting Figure 7 caption remains. The evidence supports a limited overall improvement without establishing that the revised proof resolves every theoretical issue.
